title: Hydrolysis changes particle number without creating glucose carbon
stem: P and Q are unbranched glucose-based chains of six residues each. P has alpha-glucose linkages and Q has beta-glucose linkages. An enzyme hydrolyses P but leaves Q unchanged. A sample contains 10.0 μmol of P chains; assume complete hydrolysis to glucose and ignore chain ends when discussing the shapes of long chains. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the amount of glycosidic links hydrolysed, water consumed and glucose formed in the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain enzyme selectivity and relate the long-chain versions of P and Q to storage and structural roles.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the number of dissolved solute particles before and after hydrolysis, and explain one advantage of storing glucose in large insoluble polymers.

steps.text: Each six-residue open chain contains five glycosidic links; hydrolysis consumes one water per link.
50.0 μmol links are hydrolysed and 50.0 μmol water consumed; 60.0 μmol glucose forms.
Different glucose/linkage orientation gives a different three-dimensional substrate shape; an enzyme that fits P need not fit Q.
Alpha-glucose polymers can form compact storage structures, whereas beta-glucose cellulose chains are straight and can associate into strong fibres.
Do not claim that this enzyme's failure proves Q can never be hydrolysed; another enzyme can be specific to Q.
One chain becomes six separate glucose molecules; solute particle amount changes from 10.0 to 60.0 μmol.
Particle number is sixfold, an increase of 500%, under the stated dissolved-particle model.
Large insoluble storage polymers contribute much less to osmotic effects than the same glucose inventory stored as free monomers.

title: A kink in a fatty-acid chain changes the melting behaviour of a fat
stem: Fats X and Y contain triglycerides with fatty-acid chains of equal carbon length. X contains many cis double bonds; Y contains mainly saturated chains. The plotted values are fractions of each bulk fat that are liquid after equilibration. A purified sample contains 2.00 mmol of a triglyceride with three identical fatty-acid chains. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the graph to compare the state of the fats at 20 °C and explain the difference using chain structure.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State the products and amounts after complete hydrolysis of the purified sample, and explain why a triglyceride is not a polymer.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that a more unsaturated fat always provides more insulation.

steps.text: At 20 °C, X is 80% liquid and Y is 15% liquid: a 65 percentage-point difference.
Cis double bonds produce kinks, reducing close packing between chains; saturated chains pack more closely.
Less energy is needed to disrupt interactions between the less closely packed unsaturated chains, so X melts at lower temperatures.
One triglyceride hydrolyses with three water molecules to one glycerol and three fatty acids.
2.00 mmol glycerol and 6.00 mmol fatty acid form; 6.00 mmol water is consumed.
It is assembled from glycerol and three fatty acids, not a long chain of a repeated identical monomer.
Melting behaviour alone does not determine an adipose layer's thickness or thermal resistance.
Compare equal thickness/mass and control temperature and other tissue properties; the data establish a melting difference, not a universal insulation ranking.

title: Terminal carbohydrates provide a recognition signal
stem: Fluorescent anti-A binds only the A terminal carbohydrate; anti-B binds only the B terminal carbohydrate. Equal numbers of red blood cells from sample S give signals of 90 and 80 arbitrary units; background is 5 units. Glycosidase G removes the terminal A structure without removing B. After G treatment the signals are 6 and 78. A separate protease removes the protein anchors of these particular surface molecules, releasing both carbohydrate labels. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the ABO carbohydrate pattern of S and calculate the percentage decrease in background-corrected anti-A signal after G.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how these results connect carbohydrate diversity with recognition, distinguishing the effects of G and protease.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Design a control that distinguishes enzyme specificity from general damage or unequal cell recovery.

steps.text: S displays both A and B terminal carbohydrates, consistent with AB cells.
Before G: 90−5=85; after G: 6−5=1; percentage decrease=(85−1)/85×100.
The background-corrected anti-A signal decreases by 98.8%.
Different terminal sugar arrangements give specific binding sites, so G selectively removes the anti-A recognition structure.
Protease cuts the protein component rather than hydrolysing the carbohydrate itself; loss of both labels supports their attachment to these protein anchors.
The result concerns the tested glycoproteins and does not imply every membrane carbohydrate is attached to a protein rather than a lipid.
Use an identical mock-treated sample with inactive G or buffer, equal incubation and equal counted cell numbers.
Check membrane integrity and anti-B retention; a general loss of cells or membrane would tend to reduce both signals, unlike the observed selective anti-A loss.

title: A fuel reserve must meet an energy target within a mass budget
stem: A model migratory bird needs 510 kJ from its stored organic fuel during a flight. Use 17.0 kJ g−1 for carbohydrate and 37.0 kJ g−1 for lipid; these are supplied usable-energy values. Compare dry fuel masses only. The diagram gives the usable energy carried by several dry reserve masses. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the dry mass needed if all fuel is carbohydrate or all is lipid, and the percentage mass saving from lipid.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two properties that make triglycerides suitable long-term reserves without claiming they are the only useful fuel.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate a prediction that the bird therefore loses exactly 13.8 g of total body mass on the flight.

steps.text: Required mass=510 divided by usable energy per gram.
Carbohydrate: 30.0 g; lipid: 13.8 g from an unrounded 13.7838 g.
They yield more usable energy per unit dry mass in the supplied comparison, reducing the carried mass.
Their hydrophobic insolubility allows storage without acting as many dissolved osmotic particles; adipose also contributes insulation.
Dry fuel use is not total body-mass change; water production/loss and other fuel use can change mass.
Actual energy demand, conversion efficiency and reserve accessibility vary; the arithmetic is conditional on the stated model.

title: More total protein does not guarantee an adequate amino-acid supply
stem: In a constructed dietary-protein model, a 10.0 g portion of food P releases 20 mg of essential amino acid E and 80 mg of essential amino acid F; 10.0 g of Q releases 80 mg E and 20 mg F. All other requirements are met. The daily requirement in this model is at least 60 mg of each. Assume complete digestion and additive amounts; no real foods or named amino acids are implied. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine whether 12.0 g of P alone meets both requirements and compare it with 6.00 g P plus 6.00 g Q.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why an essential amino acid can limit use of the other amino acids for a particular polypeptide.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Outline digestion of a three-amino-acid peptide into free amino acids and evaluate the model's use for real diets.

steps.text: Scale each 10 g amino-acid supply by the food mass/10.
12.0 g P provides 24 mg E and 96 mg F, so E is insufficient.
6.00 g of each provides 60 mg E and 60 mg F, meeting both requirements with the same total food mass.
Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized in sufficient amounts by the organism and must be supplied by food.
A polypeptide requires the amino acids in its specified sequence; surplus F cannot simply replace a required E.
Hydrolysis breaks two peptide bonds and consumes two water molecules to give three amino acids.
Real foods differ in digestibility and contain many amino acids/nutrients; complete digestion and only two limiting requirements are simplifications.

title: Loss and recovery of protein function need not mean chain cleavage
stem: One purified protein is measured under four treatments. Untreated activity is 100 units. Activity after heating is 20, and after cooling the heated sample is 30. A separate pH 2 treatment gives 10 units, rising to 80 after neutralization. Peptide-chain length is unchanged in every sample. Assays are performed at the same final substrate concentration and temperature except where the stated treatment is being tested. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare functional recovery after cooling and after neutralization using percentage-point changes relative to untreated activity.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why denaturation is a better interpretation than complete hydrolysis, while distinguishing loss of function from certain proof of a particular shape.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claims that denaturation is always irreversible and that all function returns whenever the original conditions are restored.

steps.text: Cooling raises activity from 20% to 30%, a 10 percentage-point recovery.
Neutralization raises activity from 10% to 80%, a 70 percentage-point recovery; it remains 20 percentage points below untreated activity.
Temperature or pH can alter the protein's conformation and hence the shape needed for its function.
Complete hydrolysis would cleave peptide chains into much smaller units, inconsistent with the unchanged measured chain length.
Activity is indirect evidence; an independent structural measurement would test the proposed conformation change.
The pH-treated sample's substantial recovery shows that the effect can be partly reversible.
Neither sample fully recovers, so restoring conditions is not a guarantee of complete functional restoration.

title: A selective barrier can admit oxygen while excluding an ion
stem: Equal-area artificial phospholipid bilayers separate two stirred solutions. Oxygen moves into the initially oxygen-free receiver. In a second system the transported species is an ion Z+. Bilayers contain no proteins unless a selective Z+ channel is added. The graph shows initial rates; the electrochemical gradient favours inward movement of Z+ when the channel is present. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the graph to distinguish simple diffusion from protein-facilitated diffusion.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict the effect of removing ATP from the external solutions and explain what would change if the gradient reversed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest two controls needed before assigning the rate difference solely to the channel.

steps.text: Oxygen crosses the protein-free bilayer, with rate increasing from 2 to 8 units as the concentration difference increases fourfold.
Small nonpolar oxygen can pass through the bilayer's hydrophobic region; charged Z+ is strongly restricted without a protein pathway.
An open Z+ channel provides a selective hydrophilic route down the supplied electrochemical gradient.
Neither simple diffusion nor an already-open passive channel directly uses ATP, so ATP removal alone need not stop these initial fluxes.
Reversing the relevant gradient reverses net passive movement; a channel is not an ATP-powered one-way pump.
Keep bilayer area, temperature, stirring and concentration/electrical gradients the same.
Use otherwise identical bilayers and check for membrane leaks; a nonselective damaged membrane could also admit ions.

title: Aquaporins change the time to osmotic equilibrium
stem: Vesicles with or without aquaporins contain the same fixed amount of an impermeant solute. They are transferred to a large external solution of twice their initial internal solute concentration. Only water can cross; pressure effects are negligible and the external concentration remains constant. Volume is expressed relative to the initial volume. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Predict the common final relative volume from solute conservation, and compare the observed volumes at 2 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the direction of net water movement and the differing rates without saying aquaporins actively pump water.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that a faster volume change proves the vesicles contain more solute.

steps.text: Internal concentration doubles when the fixed solute amount occupies half its initial volume.
Both approach relative volume 0.500.
At 2 minutes the aquaporin vesicles are 0.55 and the others 0.80, a 0.25 initial-volume-unit difference.
Net water moves out by osmosis toward the more concentrated external impermeant-solute solution.
Aquaporins increase water permeability, so the same equilibrium is approached faster; they do not use ATP to establish a different equilibrium.
The initial solute amount and concentration are controlled; permeability alone can account for the rate difference.
Measure final volumes and membrane integrity as well as initial rates; leakage of solute would violate the model.

title: ATP depletion separates uphill accumulation from a passive leak
stem: A cell contains 80 mmol dm−3 of an uncharged solute S; the external solution contains 8 mmol dm−3. Temperature, viable cell number and external concentration are held constant. Inward uptake is 6.0 units with ATP available and 0.4 after ATP depletion. The membrane also permits a small outward passive leak. Protein P spans the bilayer. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the concentration ratio and explain why sustained inward accumulation requires an energy source.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the 0.4-unit uptake does not show that all transport stops when ATP is depleted.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage decrease in measured inward uptake and propose a control testing whether ATP depletion merely killed the cells.

steps.text: Internal/external concentration=80/8.
The internal concentration is tenfold higher.
Net inward accumulation moves S against its concentration gradient; an ATP-driven pump can supply energy for this.
The rate is reduced but not zero; background binding, incomplete ATP depletion or another route may remain.
Passive outward diffusion can continue down its gradient and does not directly require ATP.
Percentage decrease=(6.0−0.4)/6.0×100.
Measured inward uptake decreases by 93.3%.
Demonstrate viability and recovery after ATP restoration, with an equal-time untreated control; cell death or nonspecific membrane damage would otherwise confound interpretation.

title: Keeping digestive enzymes in a compartment protects the cytoplasm
stem: Cells are gently homogenized in cold isotonic medium, then fractionated. Of the recovered acid-digestive-enzyme marker, 85% is in an organelle-rich pellet and 15% in supernatant. A soluble cytosolic marker is 10% in pellet and 90% in supernatant. The digestive enzyme works best at pH 5; cytoplasm is near pH 7. Intact vesicles show little activity against a large substrate outside them, but activity rises after detergent opens their membranes. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use both markers to evaluate the fractionation rather than calling the pellet pure.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the activity increase after detergent and two benefits of compartmentalization.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why cold isotonic conditions improve interpretation.

steps.text: The digestive marker is enriched in pellet, whereas the cytosolic marker is mainly in supernatant.
The pellet still contains 10% of recovered cytosolic marker and some digestive marker is outside it; cross-contamination or organelle breakage is possible.
Marker percentages describe recovery of each marker, not the percentage of pellet mass made of that organelle.
An intact membrane restricts the large substrate's access to the enzyme; detergent removes this separation.
The compartment can concentrate digestive enzymes/substrates and maintain conditions favourable for digestion.
Separation of digestion from cytoplasmic reactions limits damage to other cellular components; the pH difference also reduces activity outside the compartment.
Cold slows unwanted enzyme reactions after disruption, while isotonic medium reduces osmotic damage to organelles.
Compare detergent and untreated samples at the same assay pH; otherwise changing pH could explain the activity difference.

title: Subdivision improves exchange geometry without reducing total volume
stem: A cube-shaped cell model has side 40 μm. It is divided into eight separate cubes of side 20 μm. Each surface is fully exposed to the same medium. Use surface area=6s² and volume=s³. The cubes are geometry models, not claims that living cells are perfect cubes. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate total volume and exposed surface area before and after subdivision.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare the maximum distance from a cube's centre to its nearest surface and explain the exchange advantage.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the model for a sheet of cells whose adjacent faces touch.

steps.text: Original volume=40³; original area=6×40². For eight smaller cubes multiply each 20 μm result by eight.
Volume is 64 000 μm³ in both cases; exposed area rises from 9 600 to 19 200 μm².
Surface-area:volume ratio increases from 0.150 to 0.300 μm−1.
It decreases from 20 to 10 μm.
More exchange surface per unit volume and shorter internal diffusion distances can improve supply/removal relative to metabolic demand.
Touching faces are not fully exposed to the external medium, so summing all six faces overestimates exchange area.
Real cells differ in shape, permeability, membrane folding and internal transport; total surface area alone does not determine metabolic rate.

title: Self-renewal and differentiation are different pieces of evidence
stem: Single cells from an adult tissue niche are cultured separately. Each of 20 clones produces both replacement stem-like cells and specialized cells of three lineages normally found in that tissue. Stem-like descendants are recloned twice and continue producing both populations. No cells from unrelated organs or extra-embryonic tissues have been tested. In a model embryo strip, genetically matched cells develop different fates in a supplied concentration gradient. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain which observations support self-renewal and differentiation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Evaluate claims that the cells are multipotent, pluripotent or totipotent.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why matched cells at different positions can differentiate differently, and propose a test of the gradient's role.

steps.text: Repeated recloning with renewed stem-like descendants supports maintenance of the stem-cell population through divisions.
Production of specialized descendants of three lineages supports differentiation, rather than merely proliferation of one cell type.
The demonstrated range is consistent with multipotency within one tissue.
Three tissue lineages do not demonstrate the ability to make all body cell types required for pluripotency.
Totipotency additionally includes the capacity to form all tissues needed for a complete organism, including extra-embryonic tissues; this has not been shown.
Different signal concentrations can cause different patterns of gene expression in cells with the same genome.
Move cells or change the gradient while controlling genotype and culture conditions; a predictable fate change would test the signal's influence.
Trace single-cell descendants to exclude a mixture of already specialized starting cells masquerading as one multipotent clone.

title: A thicker alveolar barrier can outweigh a large exchange surface
stem: A simple model has oxygen transfer rate proportional to exchange area×concentration difference/barrier thickness. Tissue H has area 1.00 relative unit, concentration difference 1.00 unit and barrier thickness 1.00 μm, with transfer 240 arbitrary units. Tissue J has area 0.800, difference 0.900 and thickness 3.00 μm. Both are ventilated and perfused. This proportional model is supplied for this question. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Predict J's rate relative to H and its numerical transfer rate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish the roles of ventilation, blood perfusion and diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Measured J transfer is 80 units. Evaluate whether the model's mismatch disproves diffusion.

steps.text: The predicted relative rate is 0.240, giving 57.6 transfer units.
The greater thickness increases diffusion distance, outweighing the retained surface and gradient.
Ventilation replaces air in the lungs and helps maintain the alveolar oxygen concentration.
Perfusion brings low-oxygen blood and removes oxygenated blood, helping maintain the gradient on the blood side.
Gas exchange itself is diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier; it is not the bulk movement of air or blood.
It shows the simple model or its assumed average inputs are incomplete; it does not show oxygen is not diffusing.
Effective area, local gradients, blood flow and barrier thickness vary; measure/control these before identifying the cause of the difference.

subject: biology

title: Rapid shallow breathing can move less fresh air to exchange surfaces
stem: A model adult has 0.150 L of conducting-airway dead space per breath. Pattern P is 12 breaths min−1 with tidal volume 0.500 L; Q is 30 breaths min−1 with tidal volume 0.200 L. Use minute ventilation=frequency×tidal volume and fresh air reaching exchange regions per minute=frequency×(tidal volume−dead space). Dead-space volume and gas composition are held constant. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate total minute ventilation and fresh-air delivery for both patterns.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why equal total ventilation does not imply equal oxygen uptake.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Relate inspiration to the diaphragm and rib cage, distinguishing forced expiration from quiet recoil.

steps.text: Multiply frequency by tidal volume, then separately subtract dead space from each tidal volume before multiplying.
Both total minute ventilations are 6.00 L min−1.
Fresh-air delivery is 4.20 L min−1 for P and 1.50 L min−1 for Q.
Q spends a larger fraction of each small breath moving air in conducting passages rather than replacing gas at exchange surfaces.
Oxygen uptake also depends on the maintained oxygen gradient, barrier properties and perfusion; minute ventilation alone is insufficient.
Diaphragm contraction flattens it and external intercostal action raises the ribs, increasing thoracic volume and lowering pressure to draw air in.
Quiet expiration can follow relaxation and elastic recoil; forceful expiration additionally uses expiratory muscles such as abdominal muscles/internal intercostals.

title: Stomatal counts require a sampling unit and a leaf context
stem: One lower-epidermis field of area 0.200 mm² is counted on each of three independently grown sun leaves: 20, 24 and 16 stomata. Three independently grown shade leaves give 10, 12 and 8. Each count is one field per leaf; n=3 independent leaves per group. The schematic shows a typical dicot leaf section, not the counted surfaces. No significance test has been performed. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate mean stomatal density for each group and the percentage difference relative to shade leaves.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two leaf features supporting gas exchange and the resulting water-loss trade-off.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the counts prove sun leaves always transpire twice as fast.

steps.text: Mean counts are 20 and 10; divide each by 0.200 mm².
Sun mean=100 stomata mm−2; shade mean=50.0 stomata mm−2.
The sun-group mean is 100% higher than the shade-group mean.
Stomata connect internal air spaces with external air, while spongy mesophyll air spaces expose a large moist exchange surface.
Opening stomata permits carbon dioxide entry but also water-vapour diffusion out, so increased access for gas exchange can increase transpiration.
Stomatal aperture, size, humidity, wind and leaf temperature also affect loss; density alone does not establish the rate.
Three leaves give limited sampling, and no statistical significance follows automatically from these means.
Randomize matched genotypes to light treatments and count several fields per leaf while retaining leaf as the independent replicate.

title: Wall structure is stronger evidence of vessel identity than blood colour
stem: Two idealized circular vessel sections are drawn to the same geometric scale. Vessel X has lumen radius 4 units and outside radius 6; Y has lumen radius 6 and outside radius 7. X has much more smooth muscle and elastic tissue. Ignore tissue shrinkage for the calculations; the units are arbitrary and are not real vessel dimensions. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate wall thicknesses and the ratio of lumen areas Y:X.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce the more likely artery and vein, explaining form–function relationships.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate identification from oxygen concentration alone.

steps.text: Wall thickness is 2 units for X and 1 unit for Y.
Area ratio=π6²/(π4²).
Y:X lumen area ratio=2.25:1.
X is more likely an artery; Y is more likely a vein.
A thicker muscular/elastic wall withstands and smooths higher arterial pressures.
A vein's lower-pressure return can be assisted by skeletal-muscle compression and valves that restrict backflow.
Artery means blood travels away from the heart and vein means toward it, not a fixed oxygen content.
Pulmonary vessels are a counterexample to the systemic oxygen pattern; use structure, direction and context together.

title: A potometer follows water uptake, not every water loss directly
stem: In a sealed potometer the capillary radius is 0.500 mm. A bubble moves 5.00 mm in 10.0 min under drier air and 2.00 mm in 10.0 min after humidity is raised. Leaf area, temperature, light and air movement are controlled. Water uptake volume equals capillary cross-sectional area×bubble displacement; 1 mm³=1 μL. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate both uptake rates and their percentage decrease after humidity rises.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the humidity effect and the mechanism that moves the main transpiration stream through xylem.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate treating uptake as an exact direct measure of transpiration.

steps.text: Rate=π(0.500)²×displacement/time.
Rates are 0.393 μL min−1 and 0.157 μL min−1.
Uptake decreases by 60.0%.
Higher humidity reduces the water-vapour concentration gradient from moist leaf spaces to the air.
Evaporation from leaves produces tension; cohesion between water molecules transmits the pulling force through xylem.
Lignified xylem walls resist collapse; mature conducting vessel elements are dead and do not pump the water using ATP.
Some absorbed water may be retained in growth or changes in tissue water content, so uptake need not equal loss at every moment.
Check leaks and allow equilibration; repeat with independent shoots and standardize by leaf area.

title: A rolled dune-grass leaf alters the environment of its stomata
stem: Matched leaves of dune grass are compared under identical air movement, temperature and external humidity. Intact rolled leaves lose 2.0 g water h−1 per standardized leaf area, while experimentally held-open leaves lose 5.0 g h−1. The schematic shows the stomata on the inward-facing surface of a rolled leaf. The experiment does not measure evolutionary change. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage reduction in water loss associated with the rolled condition.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how rolling and one other structural feature can be useful in a dry dune habitat.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the comparison proves the effect is entirely due to humidity inside the roll.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Distinguish an inherited adaptation from a short-term response in this study.

steps.text: Use the held-open rate as the reference: (5.0−2.0)/5.0×100.
Water loss is 60.0% lower in the rolled condition.
Rolling shelters inward-facing stomata from wind and traps more humid air, reducing the water-vapour gradient.
A thick waxy cuticle reduces water movement through the epidermis; accept a correctly explained alternative such as hairs or reduced exposed leaf area.
Holding leaves open could damage tissue or change illumination, temperature and exposed area as well as humidity.
Use a sham manipulation, check damage and internal humidity, and control actual leaf area before assigning one causal mechanism.
An inherited capacity for leaf rolling can be an adaptation shaped over generations; rolling/unrolling by one leaf is a response, not evidence that the individual evolved.

title: Removing a competitor can reveal a broader potential niche
stem: Snail S occurs along an intertidal height gradient. Replicated plots receive either competitor removal or a sham disturbance; the graph shows mean density after one season. Sample size is eight independent plots per treatment at each height. No error bars or significance test are supplied. Temperature and immersion time also vary with height. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the range change using the plotted densities and distinguish habitat from niche.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how competition could restrict the realized niche and what the removal result cannot establish.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean-density increase at 60 cm and evaluate the strength of the causal inference.

steps.text: In sham plots S is recorded from 0 to 40 cm, while after removal it occurs from 0 to 80 cm.
Habitat is where it lives; niche includes its abiotic tolerances, resource use and interactions, not just a location.
A competitor can reduce access to resources or space, excluding S from heights it could otherwise tolerate.
Removal supports a biotic restriction on the realized niche, but the experimentally occupied range is not proof of every boundary of the fundamental niche.
At 60 cm density rises from 0 to 12 snails m−2, an absolute increase of 12; a percentage increase from zero is undefined.
Randomized replicated removal with sham disturbance is stronger than an uncontrolled correlation.
Removal might also alter shelter or predators; repeat seasons and measure these variables, and do not infer significance from means alone.

title: Both light and captured prey can contribute to one organism's nutrition
stem: One unicellular organism grows in four controlled cultures. Growth rates in divisions day−1 are: light with prey 4.0; light without prey 2.0; darkness with prey 2.0; darkness without prey 0.2. Microscopy of separate labelled cultures shows prey enclosed in food vacuoles, and a carbon tracer shows inorganic carbon incorporation in light without prey. All cultures have the same dissolved inorganic nutrients; stored reserves may support limited short-term dark growth. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the nutritional strategy from both kinds of evidence, rather than growth rate alone.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the growth-rate increase from adding prey in light and explain why the dark no-prey growth does not by itself prove a third nutritional mode.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Design controls that make the tracer and prey evidence convincing.

steps.text: It is mixotrophic: it can obtain carbon through photosynthetic fixation and by feeding on prey.
Light-dependent inorganic-carbon incorporation supports photoautotrophy, while labelled prey inside food vacuoles supports holozoic ingestion.
Relative increase=(4.0−2.0)/2.0×100.
Prey doubles the light growth rate, a 100% increase.
Stored reserves or trace organic contamination could permit short-term growth; test sustained growth over serial transfers before inferring an additional carbon source.
Use washed, labelled prey and remove free label so uptake cannot be explained by dissolved labelled carbon.
Include killed-cell or no-cell controls and matched light/dark tracer cultures; distinguish internal food vacuoles from prey merely adhering outside.

title: The same R-group property can favour a core or a membrane-spanning surface
stem: H denotes hydrophobic R-groups, P polar R-groups, and +/− charged R-groups. In soluble protein G, six of eight H residues are buried away from water; in membrane protein T, a central H-rich segment contacts the lipid bilayer. A mutation replaces one buried H residue of G with a charged residue. The mutation changes the sequence but not chain length. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the fraction of G's H residues buried, and explain the different H-rich positions in G and T.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the mutation could change tertiary conformation without breaking the peptide backbone.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Propose a test distinguishing reduced stability from reduced protein production.

steps.text: Six of eight is 0.750, or 75.0%.
In water-soluble globular proteins, hydrophobic R-groups tend to cluster internally, reducing contact with water.
A membrane-spanning protein exposes hydrophobic R-groups toward the bilayer's hydrophobic core, while hydrophilic regions can contact water.
Primary sequence fixes the positions and chemical properties of R-groups, so a charged replacement changes local interactions.
A buried charge can be unfavourable unless accommodated by suitable interactions; folding/stability can change while peptide connectivity and chain length remain.
The effect is context dependent; a sequence change does not guarantee complete denaturation.
Measure equal purified amounts of wild-type and mutant protein in a matched unfolding/function assay.
Also quantify cellular protein abundance; lower activity in whole cells alone could reflect less protein rather than changed activity per molecule.

title: Regular backbone hydrogen bonding stabilizes secondary structure
stem: A model alpha helix contains 12 residues in one uninterrupted segment. For counting only, the supplied rule is that residue i can hydrogen-bond through its backbone C=O to the backbone N–H of residue i+4, when both residues lie in the segment. The diagram shows selected backbone donors and acceptors, not all atoms. A treatment disrupts these hydrogen bonds without cleaving peptide bonds. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the possible i values and maximum number of such internal hydrogen bonds in this model.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish the bonds stabilizing the helix from the bonds connecting successive residues, and compare an alpha helix with a beta-pleated sheet.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict what can change after treatment and what cannot be concluded from an unchanged sequence.

steps.text: The last acceptor index must satisfy i+4≤12, while i starts at 1.
i=1 through 8, giving eight modeled internal hydrogen bonds.
The regular hydrogen bonds are between backbone groups; peptide bonds are covalent links joining successive amino acids.
An alpha helix is coiled; a beta-pleated sheet consists of extended pleated strands linked by regular hydrogen bonding.
Secondary-structure hydrogen bonds should not be described as a chain of peptide bonds between R-groups.
Helical organization can be lost or rearranged without changing the amino-acid order or number of peptide bonds.
Unchanged primary structure does not guarantee unchanged secondary/tertiary conformation or function; measure structure and activity separately.

title: Reducing insulin disulfides is not the same as hydrolysing its chains
stem: Mature insulin consists of chain A with 21 residues and chain B with 30. The displayed disulfides are A 6–A 11, A 7–B 7 and A 20–B 19. A reducing treatment breaks only the disulfide connections; a separate complete hydrolysis breaks all peptide bonds. No peptide bond joins A to B in mature insulin. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Count intrachain and interchain disulfides and determine the number of polypeptide chains after reduction alone.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of peptide bonds hydrolysed and water molecules consumed per insulin molecule during complete peptide hydrolysis.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the structural roles of cysteine and the two chains, and evaluate using a lost binding response as proof of peptide cleavage.

steps.text: There is one intrachain disulfide and two interchain disulfides.
Reduction leaves two polypeptide chains; it does not produce 51 free amino acids because peptide bonds have not been hydrolysed.
Each open chain has one fewer peptide bond than residues: (21−1)+(30−1).
There are 49 peptide bonds, requiring 49 water molecules to hydrolyse them.
Pairs of cysteine R-groups can form covalent disulfide bonds that help stabilize conformation and join chains.
The association of more than one polypeptide chain is quaternary organization; the disulfides also constrain their folded arrangement.
Lost receptor binding can result from changed conformation even with intact primary chains; determine chain size or peptide products to establish cleavage.

title: Protein subunits and non-protein groups answer different structural questions
stem: In a simplified separation, native haemoglobin H has protein mass 64 kDa and gives four 16 kDa polypeptide subunits after dissociation. Each subunit carries one haem group, whose mass is ignored here. Collagen C is a fibrous triple-polypeptide assembly of approximately 300 kDa, giving three approximately 100 kDa chains. The chart concerns molecular mass, not protein concentration. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the masses to calculate subunit numbers and explain why a haem group is not another polypeptide subunit.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Relate globular and fibrous organization to oxygen transport and tensile support.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate a conclusion that equal masses of H and C contain equal numbers of native protein assemblies.

steps.text: Divide native protein mass by the mass of one polypeptide.
H has four polypeptide subunits; C has three.
Haem is a non-polypeptide component, making haemoglobin a conjugated protein; it is not a fifth amino-acid chain.
Compact soluble haemoglobin has haem sites that bind oxygen reversibly and can be transported within red cells.
Long fibrous collagen assemblies give tensile strength and structural support, rather than functioning as soluble oxygen carriers.
At equal mass, molecule number is inversely proportional to molecular mass.
H:C assembly number ratio is 300/64=4.69:1, not 1:1.
The approximate masses simplify real molecular variants and associated groups; they do not by themselves measure tissue mechanical strength.

title: Cold acclimation changes membrane composition without proving a DNA change
stem: Genetically matched fish of one species are acclimated for four weeks at 5 °C or 20 °C. Unsaturated fatty-acid tails make up 60% and 30% of their membrane tails, respectively. The graph compares equal-composition model bilayers; larger fluidity-index values mean greater fluidity. All other lipid components are held constant. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the change in unsaturated-tail percentage and explain how it can compensate for low temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the model curves to evaluate the claim that the composition advantage is identical at every temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish acclimation from demonstrated evolutionary adaptation and suggest a reciprocal-transfer test.

steps.text: The cold-acclimated membranes have 30 percentage points more unsaturated tails, a 100% relative increase from 30%.
Cis unsaturated tails pack less tightly and have lower melting transitions, helping membranes remain fluid at lower temperature.
The change can oppose the stiffening caused by cooling; it does not mean cooling itself increases fluidity.
At 5 °C indices are 40 versus 15, while at 20 °C they are 70 versus 55: differences of 25 and 15 units.
The response depends on temperature and other membrane components; a fixed percentage composition does not imply a fixed fluidity difference.
A reversible change within genetically matched fish is acclimation/plasticity; this experiment does not show a heritable change in allele frequencies.
Transfer fish back to the other temperature and remeasure composition/fluidity after controlled intervals; retain independent fish as replicates.

title: Cholesterol buffers fluidity in opposite directions at opposite temperatures
stem: Model animal-cell membranes have identical phospholipids and proteins but either contain cholesterol or lack it. The fluidity index is defined so that larger values mean more fluid membrane. The curves are constructed equilibrium measurements, not universal numerical values for every membrane. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare cholesterol's effects at 5 °C and 40 °C using numerical differences.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how one molecule can have these contrasting effects, including its location.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that adding cholesterol always makes membranes more fluid, and give a limitation of this experiment.

steps.text: At 5 °C, cholesterol raises the index from 5 to 25, an increase of 20 units.
At 40 °C, cholesterol lowers the index from 80 to 55, a decrease of 25 units.
Cholesterol lies among phospholipid tails, with its small polar region near the head-group/water interface.
At low temperature it interferes with very close tail packing and helps prevent stiffening.
At high temperature it restrains phospholipid movement, reducing excessive fluidity and stabilizing the bilayer.
The high-temperature results directly contradict an always-increases claim; its effect is temperature dependent.
These matched model membranes isolate one variable but lack the full diversity of lipid/protein compositions found in living cells.

title: An extracellular protein domain becomes an endocytic luminal domain
stem: An impermeant fluorescent reagent labels an extracellular domain X of a plasma-membrane protein. After endocytosis and removal of surface label, isolated intact vesicles retain 80 fluorescence units after external protease. Detergent plus protease reduces the signal to 5. Protease cannot cross an intact bilayer. The schematic shows the membrane's sidedness; it does not show a pore opening through the cell. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the protease-protection result and calculate the fraction of fluorescence protected above the detergent/protease background.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish endocytosis from simple diffusion and predict X's orientation after the same vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether protease protection alone proves endocytosis occurred in the living cell.

steps.text: After inward budding, the former extracellular domain faces the vesicle lumen, so external protease cannot reach it.
The protected component is 80−5=75 of the 80 units retained before detergent.
The protected fraction on that definition is 75/80=93.8%.
Endocytosis encloses material by membrane budding, whereas diffusion moves individual particles through a membrane/pathway down a gradient.
Fusion returns the luminal domain to the extracellular side; membrane orientation is preserved rather than randomly flipped.
Protection supports enclosure but could also arise in sealed membrane fragments formed during isolation.
Include a time-resolved uptake assay in intact cells, a non-endocytosed surface-marker control and membrane-integrity controls to test that alternative.

title: A ligand gate and a voltage gate respond to different triggers
stem: A neuronal membrane preparation contains nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and voltage-gated sodium channels. The solution and voltage conditions make sodium entry favourable through either open pathway. Acetylcholine opens a conductance of 8.0 units; a receptor-specific antagonist reduces it to 0.2. A separate depolarizing voltage step opens sodium-channel conductance of 20 units, unchanged by that antagonist. The traces represent independent trials, not one action potential. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce which gate responds to each trigger and calculate antagonist inhibition of the acetylcholine response.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why opening a channel is not equivalent to actively pumping sodium.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate interpreting an unchanged voltage-step response as proof that the antagonist has no other cellular effect.

steps.text: Acetylcholine activates ligand-gated nicotinic receptors; the voltage step activates voltage-gated sodium channels.
The acetylcholine-evoked conductance is inhibited by 97.5%.
Opening changes permeability; sodium then moves down the supplied electrochemical gradient.
The open channel does not directly hydrolyse ATP to move sodium uphill, even though energy is needed elsewhere to maintain gradients.
It supports selectivity for the tested responses at that dose, but does not test every protein or pathway.
Use dose-response, vehicle and viability controls; the independent-trial design prevents assuming one trace caused the other.

title: An exchange pump transports unequal charges in each cycle
stem: The sodium–potassium pump uses one ATP per complete forward cycle. Each cycle exports three Na+ and imports two K+. In a short counting model it completes 800 cycles; ignore passive leaks and changes in compartment volume. The drawing places the ions on their destination sides after transport, not at binding sites inside the pump. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate ATP use, Na+ exported, K+ imported and the net positive-charge movement.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the pump's contributions to ion gradients and membrane potential, distinguishing it from channels.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate extrapolating the count to the voltage change of a living neuron.

steps.text: Multiply each stoichiometric amount by 800 cycles.
800 ATP are used; 2 400 Na+ move out and 1 600 K+ move in.
There is a net export of 800 positive elementary charges.
ATP hydrolysis supports sodium export and potassium import against their maintained electrochemical gradients.
Unequal positive-charge transfer contributes directly to an inside-negative potential; gradients also permit selective passive ion movement that helps generate membrane potential.
Channels allow downhill movement when open rather than carrying out this ATP-linked 3:2 exchange.
Charge count alone does not determine voltage without membrane capacitance and geometry.
Living cells have leaks, other transporters and changing ion distributions; the no-leak model is a short stoichiometric count, not a full voltage prediction.

title: Glucose accumulation can depend indirectly on ATP
stem: An intestinal epithelial model has an apical sodium-dependent glucose cotransporter T. Luminal sodium is 140 mmol dm−3 and cellular sodium 10; luminal glucose is 1 and cellular glucose 5. The electrochemical gradient favours sodium entry. A basolateral Na+/K+ pump maintains the sodium gradient; a separate basolateral carrier allows glucose exit when its gradient is outward. After pump inhibition, initial glucose uptake declines gradually from 60 to 10 units over 30 min rather than stopping instantly. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how T can accumulate glucose despite the glucose concentration difference.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish direct from indirect ATP dependence and explain the delayed inhibition.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate a conclusion that an ATP inhibitor acts specifically on T.

steps.text: Sodium entry down its electrochemical gradient releases free energy.
Coupling that entry to glucose entry allows glucose to move against its own concentration gradient.
The glucose concentration is fivefold greater inside, so simple inward glucose diffusion alone cannot maintain this accumulation.
The pump directly uses ATP; T uses the stored sodium gradient rather than hydrolysing ATP directly.
An existing gradient can drive transport briefly after the pump stops, then weakens as sodium redistributes.
The uptake decrease is (60−10)/60×100=83.3% after 30 min.
The inhibitor could reduce the pump's activity or other ATP-dependent cell functions, indirectly reducing T flux.
Test T with an imposed sodium gradient in a controlled membrane preparation and monitor viability/gradient to separate direct from indirect effects.

title: Cristae add membrane area while the matrix keeps a different reaction environment
stem: Two equal-volume mitochondrial preparations have the same amount of matrix-enzyme marker. Normal inner-membrane area is 40 μm² per mitochondrion and model mutant area 20 μm². Under matched substrate and oxygen conditions ATP production is 100 versus 60 units. P and Q mark fluid regions in the schematic. Do not infer that membrane area is the only altered feature of a real mutant. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify P and Q and link the compartments and cristae to aerobic respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate area and ATP-production changes and evaluate a strict proportionality claim.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why an unchanged amount of one matrix marker is useful but insufficient as a complete control.

steps.text: P is matrix; Q is intermembrane space.
Matrix compartmentalizes enzymes and substrates of the Krebs cycle.
Cristae enlarge inner-membrane area for membrane-associated ATP-producing processes; the small intermembrane volume helps maintain distinct local conditions.
Area falls by 50.0%, whereas ATP production falls by 40.0%.
ATP per stated area is 100/40=2.50 versus 60/20=3.00 units μm−2.
The values are not strictly proportional; differences in functional density, conditions or other altered properties may contribute.
It supports comparable recovery of that matrix component, helping distinguish membrane-area loss from loss of all mitochondria.
It does not establish equal amounts/activity of every enzyme, intact membranes or equal substrate transport; additional integrity and component controls are needed.

title: A large thylakoid surface is distinct from the surrounding stroma
stem: X marks the fluid enclosed inside one thylakoid; Y is outside thylakoids but inside the chloroplast envelope. Preparation A has total thylakoid-membrane area 20 μm² and enclosed thylakoid-fluid volume 0.200 μm³. Preparation B has the same area but volume 0.400 μm³. Equal photosystem content per unit membrane area and equal stromal enzyme amounts are assumed. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify X and Y and locate photosystems and Calvin-cycle enzymes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate membrane-area:enclosed-volume ratios and explain a possible benefit of small luminal volume.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that A must photosynthesize at exactly twice B's rate.

steps.text: X is thylakoid lumen; Y is stroma.
Photosystems are in thylakoid membranes; Calvin-cycle enzymes and substrates are compartmentalized in the stroma.
The double envelope separates the chloroplast from cytoplasm but is not a substitute for the internal thylakoid system.
For a given transported amount, smaller fluid volume permits a larger concentration change and helps maintain distinct conditions across the membrane.
The ratio is twice as large, but photosystem number is assumed equal because membrane area and density are equal.
Light, carbon availability, transport and enzyme rates may limit the overall rate; an area:volume ratio alone does not prove a twofold photosynthetic flux.

title: A pulse-chase follows a secreted protein through several compartments
stem: A short pulse labels newly synthesized protein P, then unlabelled amino acids are supplied. At 2, 10 and 30 min, recovered label percentages are RER 70/20/5, Golgi 10/60/10, extracellular medium 0/20/80 and other fractions 20/0/5. Each time totals 100%. A separately labelled cytosolic protein Q stays mainly outside the secretory compartments. The plotted percentages describe recovered P label, not organelle volume. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the likely route of P and explain where ribosomes synthesize P compared with Q.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the extracellular percentage-point increase between 2 and 30 min, and explain the Golgi peak without claiming Golgi makes the peptide backbone.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the time course proves every labelled molecule followed exactly that route.

steps.text: P's sequence is RER→Golgi→secretory vesicles→extracellular medium.
Membrane-bound ribosomes on rough ER synthesize proteins entering this intracellular transport/secretion route.
Free ribosomes synthesize Q for retention in the cytosolic compartment; their different location does not require a different genetic code.
Extracellular label increases by 80 percentage points.
Label first accumulates in Golgi and then leaves as processed protein moves onward in vesicles.
Ribosomes synthesize the polypeptide; Golgi processes and sorts it for secretion, rather than translating its amino-acid sequence.
Population fractions are compatible with the route but do not track every molecule individually; fraction contamination and label recycling can affect results.
Use a protein-specific assay, short chase, fraction-purity markers and controlled transport inhibition to strengthen the inference.

title: Nuclear pores allow regulated exchange across a double envelope
stem: A labelled RNA is initially detected in the nucleus. In controls, nuclear/cytoplasmic recovered label changes from 8/2 units at 2 min to 2/8 at 10 min. An export-blocking treatment gives 9/1 at 10 min, with unchanged total recovered label. Ribosomes translating this RNA are in the cytoplasm. The treatment is tested only over this short period. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the cytoplasmic fraction at 10 min in control and treated cells, and relate the change to nuclear pores.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the functional advantage of separating transcription from cytoplasmic translation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the envelope disassembles during nuclear division, and evaluate the short-term export evidence.

steps.text: Divide cytoplasmic label by total recovered label 10.
Control fraction=80%; treated fraction=10%, a 70 percentage-point difference.
Pores provide a route across the double nuclear envelope; blocked export can retain RNA in the nucleus.
New RNA can undergo post-transcriptional processing before it meets translating ribosomes.
The nuclear boundary permits different regulated activities and conditions; a pore allows exchange without removing compartmental separation.
Envelope breakdown allows chromosome attachment/segregation through the division machinery; membrane components can reassemble around daughter nuclei.
Equal total label controls recovery but not every alternative: the treatment might alter RNA degradation or processing, so measure these and cell viability before assigning a specific pore defect.

title: A coat-defective cell can still bind cargo at its surface
stem: Control cells bind 100 units of receptor-specific cargo at the surface and internalize 70 units during a short pulse. Clathrin-reduced cells bind 98 units but internalize 15. Counts are normalized per viable cell and a wash removes unbound cargo. The schematic places the coat on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate internalized cargo as a percentage of bound cargo for each condition.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the coat contributes and which step is most directly affected by these results.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether these data prove all cellular endocytosis requires clathrin.

steps.text: Use internalized/bound×100, not both values divided by control binding.
Control=70.0%; clathrin-reduced=15/98×100=15.3%.
Clathrin participates in membrane bending/formation of coated vesicles, helping concentrate selected membrane cargo.
Near-normal binding with much lower internalization supports an uptake/vesicle-formation defect rather than simple absence of surface binding sites.
The coat is cytoplasmic; cargo enclosed from outside lies in the vesicle lumen, not embedded in the clathrin coat.
Only this cargo, cell type and intervention were tested; alternative uptake mechanisms are not excluded.
Restore clathrin expression and test rescue while monitoring general membrane integrity and other cargos to support specificity.

title: Microvilli add membrane without adding a separate layer of cells
stem: An epithelial apical patch has flat area 100 μm². It develops 40 cylindrical microvilli of radius 0.100 μm and length 1.00 μm. Each top replaces an equal circular area of the original flat patch, so the net additional area is the curved side area 2πrL per microvillus. Ignore membrane thickness and end curvature. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate additional and total apical membrane area and the percentage area increase.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why microvilli can increase uptake and distinguish their organization from separate cells or cilia.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate predicting an exactly 25.1% increase in whole-tissue uptake.

steps.text: Additional area=40×2π×0.100×1.00.
Additional area=25.1 μm²; total area=125 μm² from unrounded 125.133 μm².
The area increases by 25.1%.
More membrane area can contain more transport proteins/enzymes and provide more contact with the luminal material.
Microvilli are projections of one cell's continuous membrane and cytoplasm; they are not 40 extra cells.
Their principal role here is increasing exchange/absorption surface, not beating to propel fluid as motile cilia do.
That follows only if uptake per area and all other limiting factors stay constant.
Transporter density, substrate supply, basolateral export or blood flow may limit flux; measure uptake as well as membrane area.

title: A cell type can cover most of an alveolus without being most of its cells
stem: In a model alveolar lining, thin spread cells X make up40% of cells but cover 95% of surface area. Cuboidal cells Y make up60% but cover 5%; Y contains surfactant-secreting vesicles. After selectively suppressing Y secretion, the volume increase at a fixed inflation pressure falls from 0.600 to 0.200 L. The treatment does not change haemoglobin concentration. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify X and Y and compare their average area per cell relative to one another.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the different form–function adaptations and the inflation result.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate interpreting this result as a direct measurement of haemoglobin's oxygen affinity.

steps.text: X is type I pneumocytes; Y is type II pneumocytes.
Area per X cell relative to Y=(95/40)/(5/60).
The model average area per X cell is 28.5 times that per Y cell.
Very thin type I cells minimize the gas-diffusion distance over most of the alveolar surface.
Type II secretory vesicles deliver surfactant, lowering surface tension and helping prevent alveolar collapse.
Less surfactant makes inflation harder; at the same pressure, volume increase falls by 66.7%.
The measurement concerns mechanical inflation of the air–tissue interface, not a haemoglobin dissociation curve.

title: Striations do not make cardiac and skeletal cells identical
stem: X and Y are schematic striated muscle tissues. X contains very long unbranched multinucleate fibres. Y contains shorter branched cells with central nuclei and specialized joining discs. In an equal-mass sample, mitochondrial volume fraction is 8% for X and 30% for Y. These values are constructed and do not describe every fibre subtype. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify X and Y and use two structural comparisons.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the mitochondrial volume-fraction ratio and relate it to sustained cardiac work without using it to predict ATP flux exactly.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether multinucleation alone identifies every cell as skeletal muscle.

steps.text: X is skeletal muscle; Y is cardiac muscle.
Skeletal fibres are typically long, unbranched and multinucleate, whereas cardiac cells are shorter/branched with central nuclei.
Cardiac joining discs connect neighbouring cells and support coordinated contraction; X is not simply a chain of separate one-nucleus cells.
Y:X fraction ratio=30/8.
Y has 3.75 times the mitochondrial volume fraction.
A large mitochondrial investment supports repeated aerobic ATP supply; actual ATP rate also depends on substrate, oxygen and mitochondrial activity.
Other cell types can be multinucleate, and a section can miss nuclei; use the combination of striations, fibre shape, branching and junctions.
Sampling different skeletal-fibre types or exercise histories may alter mitochondrial fractions, so independent matched samples are needed.

title: Foetal haemoglobin can load oxygen at a lower partial pressure
stem: Equal haemoglobin amounts are compared at the same temperature, pH and carbon dioxide. Curve F has P50 = 20 mmHg and curve A P50 = 27 mmHg; P50 is the oxygen partial pressure at 50% saturation. At 30 mmHg the constructed saturations are 74.93% for F and 57.06% for A. Maternal and foetal blood remain in separate vessels at the placenta. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the curve more consistent with foetal haemoglobin and quantify its saturation advantage at 30 mmHg.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how this difference aids transfer without claiming that the blood mixes or that Hb crosses the placenta.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that greater affinity is always better for an adult delivering oxygen to tissues.

steps.text: F is more consistent with foetal haemoglobin because its lower P50 indicates higher oxygen affinity.
Difference=74.93−57.06 percentage points.
Using the stated rounded values, F is 17.87 percentage points more saturated, approximately 17.9 points.
Foetal Hb binds oxygen effectively at the lower oxygen partial pressures available across the placental exchange surface.

Binding removes oxygen from the dissolved pool in foetal blood and helps maintain the dissolved-oxygen/partial-pressure gradient for further diffusion across the placental barrier; the two blood supplies remain separate.
High affinity favours loading but can reduce unloading at a given tissue oxygen partial pressure.
Effective delivery depends on the saturation difference between loading and unloading sites, Hb amount and circulation, not affinity alone.

title: A Bohr shift can increase oxygen unloading where carbon dioxide is high
stem: The same amount of adult haemoglobin is measured under low-CO2/pH 7.4 conditions with P50 = 27 mmHg and high-CO2/pH 7.2 conditions with P50 = 33 mmHg. At 40 mmHg, saturations are 74.29% and 62.70%. Temperature is held constant. Both carbon dioxide and pH differ between the two curves. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the direction of the shift and calculate the saturation difference at 40 mmHg.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the benefit in actively respiring tissues, distinguishing CO2 binding from O2 binding.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the comparison separates a direct CO2 effect from a pH effect.

steps.text: Higher CO2/lower pH shifts the dissociation curve to the right, indicating lower oxygen affinity.
Difference=74.29−62.70.
Saturation is approximately 11.59 percentage points lower in high CO2.
Respiring tissues release CO2; reduced affinity promotes oxygen dissociation where oxygen demand is high.
CO2 can bind allosterically at sites distinct from the oxygen-binding haem sites; it does not simply occupy all the same sites as oxygen.
It does not: CO2 and pH change together, so their individual contributions are confounded.
Compare CO2 levels at controlled buffered pH and pH levels at controlled CO2, with equal Hb and temperature, to separate effects.

title: A sigmoid curve carries information about cooperative binding
stem: Constructed oxygen-binding curves C and N have the same P50 = 27 mmHg and the same maximum capacity. C is cooperative haemoglobin-like binding and N is an independent-site comparison. At 10 mmHg their saturations are 6.41% and 27.03%; at 40 mmHg they are 74.29% and 59.70%. No binding equation is required. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare C and N at the two pressures, and explain why identical P50 values do not imply identical curve shapes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the S-shaped form of C in terms of subunit interactions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate C's percentage-point saturation decrease from 40 to 10 mmHg and explain why it is not itself a volume of oxygen.

steps.text: At 10 mmHg C is less saturated (6.41% versus 27.03%), but at 40 it is more saturated (74.29% versus 59.70%).
P50 specifies one point, not the full response at other pressures.
Binding of an initial oxygen molecule alters haemoglobin conformation.
This increases the tendency of remaining haem groups to bind oxygen, producing a steep central part of the curve.
At high oxygen pressure most sites are occupied, so the curve levels off; the plateau is not evidence of unlimited extra binding sites.
Subtract 6.41% from 74.29%.
From the supplied rounded values, the decrease is 67.88 percentage points, approximately 67.9.
Converting a fractional saturation change to oxygen volume requires the amount of haemoglobin and its oxygen capacity.

title: Oxygen content depends on both affinity and haemoglobin amount
stem: Blood models X and Y are compared at the same temperature and CO2. X contains 100 g Hb L−1 with P50 = 27 mmHg; Y contains 120 g Hb L−1 with P50 = 35 mmHg. Each gram of fully saturated Hb binds 1.34 mL oxygen. At 40 mmHg, fractional saturations are 0.7429 and 0.5892. Ignore dissolved oxygen for the calculation. These are models, not clinical diagnostic data. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Distinguish which model has higher affinity and which has higher maximum oxygen capacity per litre.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate oxygen bound per litre at 40 mmHg using the supplied rounded fractional saturations.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate identifying foetal blood from a single measured oxygen content.

steps.text: X has higher affinity because its P50 is lower; Y has more Hb and hence higher full-saturation capacity.
Full capacities=Hb concentration×1.34.
X capacity=134 mL L−1; Y capacity=160.8 mL L−1.
Bound content=full capacity×fractional saturation.
X≈99.55 and Y≈94.74 mL L−1; accept small differences from unrounded curves.
More Hb in Y partly compensates for lower affinity, but does not guarantee higher content at every oxygen pressure.
Content confounds Hb amount, saturation and oxygen conditions; a high content alone is not a measurement of high affinity.
Compare controlled dissociation curves/P50 and Hb concentration, rather than assigning developmental identity from one content value.

title: Lymphatic drainage closes a tissue-fluid budget
stem: A simplified steady local model has 20 mL min−1 leaving blood capillaries for tissue fluid, 17 returning directly to blood and 3 entering lymph vessels. These rates are supplied aggregate exchanges, not a claim that every real capillary has this exact pattern. A partial lymph blockage lowers drainage to 1 mL min−1 while other rates initially stay unchanged. Plasma proteins are largely retained in blood in the unblocked model. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Verify the initial balance and calculate the initial accumulation rate and one-hour accumulation after blockage, if rates remained fixed.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain capillary exchange, protein retention and the lymphatic return route.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate extrapolating the initial model for many hours and predict the effect of increased protein leakage.

steps.text: Steady balance:20−17−3=0. After blockage:20−17−1.
Initial accumulation is 2 mL min−1; conditional one-hour accumulation is 120 mL.
Capillary walls are thin and allow exchange of water and small solutes between blood and tissue fluid.
Retained plasma proteins favour water retention/return toward blood by osmotic effects; pressure also affects outward movement.
Excess tissue fluid enters thin-walled lymph vessels with gaps and valves, then returns to blood circulation rather than being permanently lost.
Accumulated fluid changes tissue pressure and exchange rates, so a fixed 2 mL min−1 long-term prediction is unlikely to remain accurate.
Loss of plasma proteins into tissue reduces the osmotic difference favouring water retention in blood and can promote tissue-fluid accumulation; consider the altered pressures too.

title: Valve positions follow pressure differences rather than a timetable alone
stem: The graph gives left-atrial, left-ventricular and aortic pressures during one constructed cardiac cycle. At 0.10 s they are 12, 15 and 78 mmHg; at 0.20 s10, 100 and 85; at 0.40 s8, 70 and 95; at 0.50 s10, 5 and 85. End-diastolic ventricular volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume 50 mL. Heart rate is 75 min−1. Use cardiac output=stroke volume×heart rate. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce mitral and aortic valve states at 0.20 and 0.50 s from the pressure differences.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why both valves can be closed at 0.10 and 0.40 s and identify the event initiating the heartbeat.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate stroke volume and cardiac output, and distinguish them from ejection pressure.

steps.text: At 0.20 s ventricular pressure exceeds atrial and aortic pressures, closing the mitral valve and opening the aortic valve.
At 0.50 s atrial pressure exceeds ventricular while aortic pressure exceeds ventricular, opening the mitral valve and closing the aortic valve.
At both times ventricle pressure exceeds atrium but remains below aorta; neither pressure gradient opens its corresponding forward valve.
The sinoatrial node initiates the heartbeat; valves respond passively to pressure differences rather than actively pumping blood.
Stroke volume=120−50=70 mL; output=70×75.
Cardiac output=5 250 mL min−1=5.25 L min−1.
Pressure is force per area, whereas stroke volume and output measure volume per beat and per time; pressure alone does not determine either.

title: Two heart passages can restore pressure between two capillary beds
stem: Circuit 1 represents a bony fish: one pump sends blood through gills, then body, then back to the pump. Circuit 2 represents a mammal: pump Q sends blood to lungs and pump R sends it to body. Q and R are the two sides of one heart, not two separate organs. Vessel directions are shown. Constructed pressures after a gas-exchange bed are 12 mmHg in circuit 1 and 25 mmHg in circuit 2's pulmonary route; mammalian systemic arterial pressure is 120 mmHg. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify single and double circulation, and identify Q and R as right or left heart.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Trace one mammalian red cell from vena cava to aorta, naming the chambers and pulmonary vessels in order.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the pressure advantage and calculate the stated systemic:pulmonary pressure ratio without treating it as an oxygen-concentration ratio.

steps.text: Circuit 1 is single circulation; circuit 2 is double circulation.
Q is right heart to lungs; R is left heart to body.
Vena cava→right atrium→right ventricle→pulmonary artery→lung capillaries.
Then pulmonary vein→left atrium→left ventricle→aorta; valves and septum maintain directed, separated flow.
A second passage through the heart can raise pressure again after pulmonary capillaries, supplying high-pressure systemic flow while keeping pulmonary pressure lower.
The supplied pressure ratio is 4.80:1.
Pressure is not oxygen concentration, and these values do not imply that fish blood lacks oxygen or that the two mammalian sides normally mix.
