title: Root pressure and phloem loading use living cells in different ways
stem: At night in humid air, a rooted plant develops positive xylem pressure 40 kPa. A reversible root ATP-production inhibitor lowers it to 10 kPa; after washing out the inhibitor it recovers to 35 kPa. Transpiration remains very low throughout. A separate diagram shows a phloem sieve-tube element and companion cell. These are not the same conduits as xylem vessels. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial pressure reduction and explain a mechanism for positive root pressure at low transpiration.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain three phloem form–function features, distinguishing sieve elements from companion cells.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the inhibitor evidence and the claim that all upward xylem flow is ATP-pumped by dead vessels.

steps.text: Pressure decreases by 75.0%.
Active mineral-ion transport into root xylem increases solute accumulation, drawing water inward by osmosis and generating positive pressure when transpiration pull is small.
Sieve plates with pores and reduced cytoplasm/organelles ease sap flow between sieve-tube elements.
Mature sieve elements lack a nucleus, while living companion cells have many mitochondria to support their metabolic/transport roles.
Plasmodesmata connect companion cells with sieve elements, supporting loading/unloading and maintenance.
Partial recovery supports a reversible energy-dependent root process, but broad ATP inhibition can affect several living-cell functions; monitor viability and ion transport.
Mature xylem conduits are dead; most daytime transpiration flow is pulled by cohesion-tension, while living root cells can create root pressure under these conditions.

title: Shorter sarcomeres do not require shorter actin or myosin filaments
stem: The same model sarcomere changes from length 3.00 μm to 2.20 μm. Thick filaments are 1.60 μm long and each thin filament extends 1.00 μm inward from its Z line in both states. All filaments are centred/aligned as drawn. Use the central region lacking thin filament length=L−2.00 μm for these two states. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the geometry to explain sliding-filament contraction rather than filament shortening.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why relaxation/stretching involves titin and antagonistic muscles rather than active pushing by a contracted muscle.

steps.text: Shortening=(3.00−2.20)/3.00×100; central length=L−2.00.
Sarcomere shortening is 26.7%; central lengths decrease from 1.00 to 0.200 μm.
Thin filaments slide farther between the thick filaments, increasing overlap and bringing Z lines closer.
Thick and thin filament lengths stay 1.60 and 1.00 μm; it is their relative position and sarcomere length that change.
Titin provides elastic recoil after stretch and helps prevent sarcomere overstretching.
Muscles generate pulling force when they contract; an antagonist can pull a bone/body part in the opposite direction and stretch the first muscle.
Reduced activation permits relaxation but does not make the same muscle actively push its attachments apart.

title: Recruiting whole motor units gives a stepped force record
stem: In a simplified preparation, increasing stimulus level recruits motor units in a fixed order. At levels 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 the total force is 0, 12, 32, 62 and 62 N. Each newly recruited unit adds a constant force, and already recruited units retain their force; firing frequency and muscle length are fixed. The schematic shows three motor neurons and their separate fibre groups, but fibre drawing count is not a force calibration. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the force contribution of each unit and explain the final plateau.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the structural meaning of a motor unit and why whole-muscle force can be graded.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether exactly 42 N can be selected by stimulus level in this fixed-order model.

steps.text: Subtract successive total forces:12−0, 32−12, 62−32.
Unit forces are 12, 20 and 30 N; level 4 adds no further force.
Under the stated model, all available units have been recruited by level 3, so further stimulus amplitude cannot recruit another unit.
A motor unit is one motor neuron and the skeletal muscle fibres it innervates, connected through neuromuscular junctions.
Recruiting additional units increases the number of active fibres; an all-or-none response of an individual unit does not make the whole muscle's force all-or-none.
No tested/modelled recruitment state gives 42 N: the successive states are 0, 12, 32 and 62 N.
Although 12+30=42 arithmetically, fixed recruitment order does not permit unit 3 without unit 2.
Real muscle can also alter firing frequency, length and activation pattern; the restricted model does not prove 42 N is impossible in every physiological situation.

title: A small muscle moment arm requires a large force at a joint
stem: A simplified static hip lever has a 60.0 N load acting 40.0 cm from the pivot and muscle force acting 4.00 cm from it. Both forces are perpendicular to the lever and act in opposite rotational directions. Ignore limb weight. Use moment=force×perpendicular distance and equate opposing moments. The biological joint is the ball-and-socket connection of the femur with the pelvis. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate load moment and the muscle force needed for equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the distinct roles of tendons, ligaments, cartilage and synovial fluid in the actual hip.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A goniometer records maximum flexion 120° before a restriction and 85° after. Calculate the change and evaluate the lever's anatomical limits.

steps.text: Load moment=60.0×0.400 N m; muscle force×0.0400 equals that moment.
Load moment=24.0 N m and muscle force=600 N.
Tendons transmit pulling force from muscle to bone; ligaments connect bones and help limit excessive joint displacement.
Articular cartilage and synovial fluid reduce friction and support smooth movement between the femoral head and pelvic socket.
The recorded range is reduced by 35°, or 29.2% relative to 120°.
A ball-and-socket hip moves in several planes; one flexion angle does not measure all its range of motion.
Real moment arms vary with joint angle and several muscles/limb weight contribute; the 600 N result belongs to the stated static model, not a full anatomical prediction.

title: Streamlining can reduce the power needed for a migration speed
stem: Equal-volume models of a marine mammal's streamlined body and a less-streamlined comparison are towed at the same speeds. At 2.00 m s−1 their drag forces are 40.0 and 65.0 N. Use mechanical power against drag=drag force×speed. This mechanical model excludes muscle efficiency, buoyancy changes and metabolic maintenance. Real marine mammals propel themselves using muscular body/tail movements and use flippers for control. All measurements in this question are constructed for this practice task; diagrams are original schematics, not micrographs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate towing powers at 2.00 m s−1 and the percentage power reduction associated with the streamlined shape.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Relate two marine-mammal features to swimming and explain why muscle action must be coordinated rather than a muscle pushing back on its own.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate extrapolating the power difference to a 38.5% reduction in total migration energy.

steps.text: Power=force×speed.
Powers are 80.0 W and 130 W.
Streamlining reduces resistance; modified limbs/flippers assist steering/stability, and muscular tail/body movements produce propulsion.
Muscles pull on contraction; coordinated opposing muscle groups can reverse movement while elastic structures assist return, rather than one muscle actively pushing its attachments apart.
Only drag power at a fixed speed is compared; total energy also includes duration, metabolic maintenance and conversion efficiency.
Real animals change speed, depth, behaviour and propulsive efficiency; measure whole-animal energy use and travel conditions before making that quantitative claim.
